Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
The world is a dangerous place
My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

vignette: Mateo was twenty-four when the assault occurred during a family reunion. He had stepped into the unheated laundry room of his relative's house to wait for a glass of water. The specific temperature on his forearms, the exact chill of the tile seeping through his dress shoes, remains seared into his recall. The door clicked shut behind him. He does not remember the encounter as something completed years ago; the memory arrives unbidden during morning routines or while he is reviewing files, forcing its way into his mind with such clarity that his skin still tenses when a draft catches his wrists. He carries a heavy sense of contamination, certain that the dirt of what happened can never be fully washed away. Alongside this, he holds the conviction that his body has been permanently damaged. These realities sit with him, unbroken by time, occupying the same mental space without intersecting. As a prosecutor, Mateo's professional environment became the stage where his daily patterns took root. He developed a steady habit of avoiding unfamiliar courtrooms and municipal offices, telling himself he could not assess the danger in unknown spaces. At the same time, scanning for exits became automatic; he mapped the nearest route out the moment he crossed any threshold. His attention naturally fixed on potential weapons: the heavy letter openers on conference tables, the glass display cases in the clerk's lobby, the metal fire extinguishers mounted near the loading docks. These behaviors did not replace one another; they ran together, layering over his routine. When the building's HVAC system dropped the temperature, that precise sensation on his skin would arise independently, and he would abruptly leave meetings under the pretense of an urgent deadline. The accumulation of these experiences reshaped his personal life. He stopped attending family gatherings because the presence of related people brought the old violation forward with undeniable force. His two adult children live only two hours away, but he no longer visits their homes. Being around their young grandchildren brings a sharp awareness of physical vulnerability, while the warmth of their house's radiators mirrors the exact temperature that precedes his distress. He does not link these sensations to one another; they simply arise side by side, making the household feel impossible to navigate. His wife's passing five years ago left the house quiet, and he has carried the isolation alone, reading newspapers for reports of violence and walking through his neighborhood with his shoulders permanently tightened, certain that the world is a dangerous place. Now at sixty-seven, Mateo sits in the quiet of his study, surrounded by case files he has stopped accepting. The uncontrolled access of the memories has begun to fracture his sleep, and the parallel weight of contamination and vulnerability has grown too heavy to bear alone. He walked into the clinic last Tuesday because he could no longer navigate his days without counting doors or waiting for the temperature to shift. He is afraid that speaking about the past will seal the contamination permanently, that the danger he expects will finally arrive. Yet, beneath the fear, he hopes someone can help him find a way to sit in a room without the memories forcing their way forward, so he might finally rest.
